svg.title: Nested virtualization layers: local source lab and AWS target
svg.desc: Left: laptop, Windows 11, VMware Workstation, nested ESXi, future source VM. Right: AWS Nitro, EC2 instance with Linux KVM and Kubernetes, KubeVirt, QEMU/KVM, target VM. L0, L1 and L2 labels.
svg.text: Nested virtualization: where each layer runs
LOCAL SOURCE LAB (built, observed)
L2
Future source VM: legacy-source-vm (PLANNED)
small Linux + nginx; vmxnet3 + pvscsi; VMDK on migration-datastore
runs on nested ESXi's VMM (uses VT-x exposed by Workstation)
L1
Nested ESXi 8.0.3 (esxi-8-lab), build 24677879
8 vCPU, 16 GB, HV Support = 3 (VT-x visible to ESXi)
vmk0 192.168.50.11 static; migration-datastore VMFS-6 199.8 GB
a guest of Workstation with vhv.enable = TRUE
L0
VMware Workstation Pro 17.6.4 (hypervisor, CPL0 mode)
VMnet8 NAT 192.168.50.0/24; runs ESXi as a VM
hosted on Windows 11 (hypervisorlaunchtype Off, VBS/HVCI off)
Physical laptop
Intel Core i7-14650HX, 16 cores / 24 threads, 32 GB RAM
VT-x + EPT enabled in firmware
AWS TARGET (PLANNED, not created)
L2
Target VM (migrated legacy-source-vm)
same guest OS, now on virtio devices, disk on a PVC
QEMU process inside a virt-launcher Pod
L1
EC2 instance = Kubernetes worker node
Linux kernel with KVM module, /dev/kvm present
kubelet + containerd
KubeVirt: virt-handler, virt-launcher Pods
CDI importer Pods, EBS CSI volumes
Needs a nested-virtualization instance type
(e.g. M8i/C8i/R8i/M7i families, NestedVirtualization=enabled)
or a *.metal instance, where this becomes L0
L0
AWS Nitro hypervisor on AWS hardware
passes Intel VT-x through to the instance when
nested virtualization is enabled (Feb 2026 onward)
we never see or control this layer
Terminology
L0 = the hypervisor that owns the real CPU. L1 = a guest hypervisor running inside an L0 VM. L2 = a VM run by the L1 hypervisor.
VT-x lets a hypervisor run guest code directly on the CPU; EPT gives each guest its own hardware-walked memory page tables.
For L1 to run L2 with hardware acceleration, L0 must expose (emulate) VT-x/EPT to L1. Every L2 VM exit is handled by L0 first, then reflected to L1.
Why this is a lab architecture
Local: two hypervisors are stacked on a laptop CPU with P/E cores, sharing 32 GB with Windows. Good for learning, not for performance numbers.
AWS: nested KVM on Nitro is supported but AWS recommends bare metal for performance-sensitive workloads. Fine for a disposable demo.
